title: Echad Mi Yodea
description: Echad Mi Yodea ("Who Knows One?"), the counting song sung near the end of the Passover Seder, in Hebrew to the minor tune the Union Haggadah printed in 1923, in four parts of our own. Each verse asks who knows a number and answers with what it stands for, counting back down to one: four mothers, three fathers, the two tablets of the covenant, and the one, Hashem, in heaven and on earth. Sung here from one to four.

credits.words: traditional Hebrew counting song of the Passover Haggadah

licence.words: public domain: traditional, anonymous (part of the Haggadah since about the fifteenth century, as the Union Haggadah's notes say)
licence.tune: public domain: traditional, printed without a composer in the Union Haggadah (1923)
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella. Accepted exceptions (singable.py): the bass's average pitch sits a hair (a twentieth of a semitone) under the beginner bass's middle, from its low opening F.
licence.source: melody and words from The Union Haggadah: Home Service for the Passover, revised edition (edited and published by the Central Conference of American Rabbis, copyright 1923; the music 'as edited by the Society of American Cantors'), p. 93, 'Ehod Mi Yodea', in D minor, 4/4 with an eighth-note pickup, voice and piano, no composer printed; written here in F minor, a minor third up, so the tune (C-sharp 4 to B-flat 4 as printed, E4 to D-flat 5 here) sits in the soprano's range and the last chord has room for all four parts; the piano part used only to check the chords. The print sets stanzas 1 and 2 under the notes, its third bar marked '(Omit for first stanza)' and, as we read it, sung once for each number counted back to two; stanzas 1 to 4 are sung here, their Hebrew as the print gives it on p. 87 (its Hebrew for eight and nine, on p. 89, is the Reform text, 'eight days of Hanukkah' and 'nine festivals', but those stanzas aren't sung here). The words are respelled from the print's Ashkenazi transliteration ('Ehod', 'Sh'-na-yim', 'luhos hab'ris') in modern Israeli pronunciation (' only where the shva has no note of its own, 'sh'nei', 'sh'lo-sha'; where it has one, it is spelled e, 'She-na-yim'); the print underlays only stanzas 1 and 2, so the later numbers are fitted to its notes by us, with the stressed syllables on the beats where the tune allows; stanza 2's counting bar is underlaid a note earlier than the print ('sh'nei' on one note, where the print gives 'sh'-ne' two) and stanza 3's 'sh'lo-sha' follows stanza 4's underlay, so the stresses fall on beats on its opening and answer lines (in the counting bars, 'sh'lo-sha' and 'ar-ba' take the two repeated Cs, as the print's own stanza 2 'sh'-ne' does). Breaths written in for beginners, as the tune has no rest until each stanza's end: before a new number, the counting bar's last two eighths become a rest; before 'e-chad e-lo-kei-nu' after a breath, the counting bar's beat-4 note is left out and its last eighth becomes a sixteenth, so 'e-' comes a sixteenth late (in stanzas 2 to 4); in stanza 1 the answer's quarter note is split into two eighths for 'de-a' to make room for that breath; each stanza's last note, which the print holds with a fermata, is held, with a bar added for the breath before the next, and the song's last note to the bar line. Read from the scan at archive.org/details/unionhaggadahhom00unse (leaf n112; the Hebrew on leaf n106); divine names in substituted forms (Hillel, 2026-11-11), the forms customary when singing outside prayer: Elokeinu, as the custom is.
